title: Electromagnetic waves in free space
prior_knowledge_summary: A transverse wave has oscillations perpendicular to its direction of energy transfer.
Wave speed, frequency and wavelength are related by v = f lambda.
The immediately previous lesson used prediction and calculation to connect a wave model with a detected frequency.
new_learning: Every electromagnetic wave travels at the same speed c in free space.
Use c = f lambda for electromagnetic waves in free space.
not_yet_taught: The order and approximate wavelength ranges of electromagnetic-spectrum regions.

blocks.heading: How can a message cross empty space?
content: Sound needs matter to carry its vibrations. Yet a spacecraft can send a radio message across the near-vacuum between planets. What is travelling when there are almost no particles to vibrate?
The answer is an electromagnetic wave. Its oscillating quantities are electric and magnetic fields, so it does not need a material medium.

figure.purpose: Create the need for a wave that can transfer a signal through free space.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper colourful teacher sketch. Show Earth and a small spacecraft separated by mostly empty space. A radio pulse crosses the gap while a crossed-out row of air particles shows that no material medium is required. Keep labels sparse.
figure.alt_text: A radio pulse travels between a spacecraft and Earth through free space without air particles.

blocks.heading: One family, one transverse behaviour
content: Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays may seem very different. They are all electromagnetic waves.
Every electromagnetic wave is transverse. The electric-field and magnetic-field oscillations are perpendicular to the direction in which energy travels.

This recalls the controlled definition: a transverse wave is a wave in which the displacement of particles is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer. For an electromagnetic wave there are no vibrating material particles in free space, so we describe perpendicular field oscillations instead.

controlled_definition.accepted_definition: a wave in which the displacement of particles is perpendicular to the direction of energy transfer

figure.purpose: Separate field-oscillation direction from energy-transfer direction.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper teacher sketch. Draw a horizontal energy-transfer arrow, a vertical electric-field oscillation and a perpendicular magnetic-field oscillation suggested by short depth arrows. Mark the right angles clearly without making a polished 3D scene.
figure.alt_text: Electric and magnetic field oscillations are perpendicular to the direction of electromagnetic-wave energy transfer.

blocks.heading: One speed in free space
content: All electromagnetic waves travel with the same speed in free space. We use the symbol c for this speed: $c=3.00\times10^8$ m s$^{-1}$.
Changing the frequency does not change the free-space speed. Instead, frequency and wavelength change together so their product remains c.
Free space matters. This common-speed statement is not a claim that every electromagnetic wave has the same speed inside every material.

figure.purpose: Show that different frequencies share one free-space speed while having different wavelengths.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper comparison strip. Draw three stylised electromagnetic wave traces with low, medium and high frequency over equal travel arrows. Label every travel arrow c and show wavelength decreasing as frequency increases. Do not name spectrum regions.
figure.alt_text: Three electromagnetic waves have different frequencies and wavelengths but the same free-space speed c.

blocks.heading: Find the wavelength of a free-space signal
content: The formula to remember is $v=f\lambda$. Here v is wave speed in m s$^{-1}$, f is frequency in Hz and $\lambda$ is wavelength in m.
For an electromagnetic wave in free space, replace v by c. A signal has frequency $2.40\times10^9$ Hz, so $\lambda=c/f=(3.00\times10^8)/(2.40\times10^9)=0.125$ m.
A unit check supports the result: (m s$^{-1}$)/(s$^{-1}$) gives m. Substitution back gives $(2.40\times10^9)(0.125)=3.00\times10^8$ m s$^{-1}$.

figure.purpose: Model rearrangement, substitution, units and an independent product check.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper worked layout with four rows: set v equal to c, rearrange for wavelength, substitute values with units, then multiply frequency by wavelength to check c. Add a small 0.125 m bracket on a wave trace.
figure.alt_text: A worked free-space wave calculation obtains a wavelength of 0.125 metres and checks the product f lambda.

blocks.heading: Use the same rule in reverse
content: Now suppose a free-space electromagnetic wave has wavelength $6.00\times10^{-7}$ m. The same common speed applies, so $f=c/\lambda$.
The very large frequency is reasonable because the wavelength is extremely small. Multiplying the result by $6.00\times10^{-7}$ m returns $3.00\times10^8$ m s$^{-1}$.

figure.purpose: Reinforce reverse use of the wave equation and scale reasoning.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper annotated calculation card. Show a tiny wavelength bracket, rearrangement to f equals c divided by wavelength, powers-of-ten substitution and a final product check. Do not classify the wave by spectrum region.
figure.alt_text: A wavelength of six times ten to the minus seven metres gives a frequency of five times ten to the fourteen hertz in free space.

blocks.heading: Higher frequency does not mean faster in free space
content: It is tempting to imagine that a more rapidly oscillating wave must race ahead. That idea works neither from the common-speed rule nor from $c=f\lambda$.
When frequency rises in free space, wavelength falls by the matching factor. For example, doubling f halves $\lambda$, so the product and speed stay unchanged.

Another tempting picture is particles bobbing inside empty space. Electromagnetic waves instead involve oscillating fields. Their transverse nature refers to field direction, not the motion of material particles.

figure.purpose: Correct both the higher-frequency-means-faster error and the particle-oscillation picture.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper error clinic. Pair a low-frequency long-wavelength wave and a doubled-frequency half-wavelength wave arriving together, both labelled c. Beside them cross out material particles and replace them with field arrows.
figure.alt_text: Doubling frequency halves wavelength so two electromagnetic waves still travel together at speed c in free space.

blocks.heading: The free-space electromagnetic-wave model
content: Use three linked statements. Every electromagnetic wave is transverse. It needs no material medium. In free space every member of the family travels at $c=3.00\times10^8$ m s$^{-1}$.
For calculations, start with the controlled formula $v=f\lambda$, set $v=c$, convert every quantity to SI units and solve for the unknown.
Finish by checking that frequency multiplied by wavelength returns c. The next lesson will attach names and approximate wavelength ranges to the family, but those ranges are not needed yet.

figure.purpose: Unify transverse behaviour, no-medium travel, common speed and the calculation routine.
figure.brief: Rectangular white-paper concept map. Centre card says electromagnetic waves in free space. Branches lead to transverse fields, no material medium, common speed c, and calculation path v equals f lambda then v equals c then SI conversion then product check.
figure.alt_text: A concept map links transverse fields, travel without a medium, common speed c and the free-space wave calculation routine.
